summary:
Ezekiel was a priest deported to Babylonia in 597 BC with Judah's king Jehoiachin. The book opens among the exiles — Judeans carried off from their homeland — by the River Kebar, a Babylonian canal (1:1–3), and stamps its visions with dates, from roughly 593 to 571 BC (1:2; 29:17). The first vision: four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings; wheels like "a wheel within a wheel," their rims "full of eyes all around"; above them a throne bearing "the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD" (1:16–28). Jewish tradition later restricted study of this "chariot" (merkabah) vision (Mishnah, Hagigah 2:1). God addresses Ezekiel again and again as "son of man" — Hebrew ben-adam, simply "human." He eats a scroll of "words of lamentation, mourning, and woe" that tastes "as sweet as honey" (2:10; 3:3) and is appointed a "watchman for the house of Israel" (3:17).

Until Jerusalem falls the message is judgment, often acted out in sign-acts (symbolic performances): Ezekiel models the besieged city on a brick, lies on his side for 390 days, and shaves his head with a sword, dividing the hair into thirds — burned, slashed, scattered (4–5). In a vision he watches "the glory of the LORD" leave the temple in stages, finally stopping over the mountain east of the city (10–11). Chapter 18 rejects a proverb blaming the children for the fathers' sins: "The soul who sins is the one who will die" (18:4). When Ezekiel's wife dies, God forbids him to mourn — a sign of the stunned grief coming on the exiles (24:15–24). Judgments on seven neighboring nations follow (25–32), among them a lament casting the king of Tyre as a cherub expelled from Eden — Satan's fall to some readers, exalted royal imagery to others (28). Then a fugitive from Jerusalem brings the news: "The city has been taken!" (33:21).

With the city fallen, the book turns to restoration. Israel's rulers, indicted as shepherds who fed themselves rather than the flock, will be replaced: "I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David" (34:23) — language echoed when Jesus says "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). God promises, "I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh" (36:26). In a valley of dry bones God asks, "can these bones come to life?" (37:3); as Ezekiel prophesies, the bones reassemble, breath enters them, and "a vast army" stands — "these bones are the whole house of Israel" (37:11). A last invasion by "Gog of the land of Magog" is destroyed (38–39); Revelation 20:8 reuses the names for the final battle.

The closing vision (40–48) tours a new temple measured in detail — whether literal blueprint, symbol, or idealized picture remains debated. Into it "the glory of the LORD" returns through the east gate and fills the temple (43:4–5), reversing the departure of chapters 10–11. From under the threshold a river flows east — ankle-deep at first, then "deep enough for swimming" (47:5) — freshening the Dead Sea, lined with trees whose fruit "will be used for food and their leaves for healing" (47:12), a picture Revelation 22:1–2 reuses for its river of life. The land is redivided among the twelve tribes, and the book's last words rename the city: "and from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE" (48:35).
